first.rationale: The two measurable declines (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) point at the same funnel stage, and memory_86 plus memory_31 are the two inherited records that speak directly to it, so the single slot is best spent there rather than on the competitor headline. I want memory_86 verified first because it is the closest match to the primary intended action and its summary reports only proximal outcomes (completion rate, time-to-value, 'early adoption') with no statement about qualified revenue or retention downstream; I need the original record to see whether downstream value was ever measured or merely assumed. memory_31 is verified second because 'cutting required fields at signup' is exactly the kind of intervention that can lift activation while degrading lead qualification data and therefore sales-qualified revenue quality; the summary's claim of a 'durable' lift needs a stated measurement window to be trusted. memory_73 is verified third as the live alternative: promotional pricing is the intuitive answer to a competitor's entry pricing, and if its source record shows lift measured on retained margin-bearing revenue rather than acquisition counts, I should reconsider. But as summarized it carries the clearest downstream risk — discount-acquired price-sensitive SMBs tend to churn or anchor low, converting a headline acquisition win into weaker long-run qualified revenue, and it does nothing about the funnel decay that would still be there next quarter. Enterprise sales-assist (memory_44) is off-target for the SMB pressure and does not touch the declining metrics; referral incentive (memory_57) is scoped to established customers and cannot repair a top-of-funnel leak; activation_messaging (memory_91) is the strongest fallback and is why I keep it in scope, but it treats the symptom downstream of the onboarding drop rather than the drop itself. Important caveat: all six items are consolidated summaries of archived records, and consolidation strips effect sizes, sample sizes, durations, and the conditions under which each result held. Two of them are over two months old, and the environment has since changed (new competitor, declining funnel), so prior lifts may not replicate. I am treating these as priors, not findings. Standard experiment scale rather than broad rollout: the direction is well supported by two independent inherited records, but the downstream-value question is genuinely open, so the test must instrument qualified-revenue and lead-quality metrics — not just completion rate — and shorten onboarding without deleting qualification fields. If verification shows memory_86's lift was proximal-only or short-window, I will drop to a small guarded test or pivot to activation_messaging.

final.rationale:
Verification largely confirmed the funnel direction and decisively killed the tempting alternative. exp_86 holds: completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and crucially 30-day retention +3%, so the shortened-onboarding lift is not purchased at the cost of cohort quality. exp_31 also holds on the relevant segment: signup +15%, activation +9%, qualified revenue +4%, with 30-day retention only -1% — a real but small drag, and the qualified-revenue number means the effect was measured downstream rather than assumed. Two independent records pointing at the same stage, both instrumented past the proximal metric, is the strongest support available for any candidate, and that stage is exactly where the current declines are (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%).

The decisive finding is exp_73. The consolidated summary said 'strong acquisition and revenue lift' and omitted 30-day retention -12% and an explicit source-record instruction not to generalize targeted discounting as sustainable growth. The acquired cohort does not survive first renewal. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, promotional_pricing is not merely weaker than it looked — it is contraindicated by its own source record, and the +18% qualified revenue figure is a pre-renewal artifact. Matching the competitor's entry pricing would buy a quarter of headline signups and hand back the cohort at renewal while the funnel leak stayed unrepaired.

That gap between summary and source is the main thing I carry forward to the unverified items. memory_44, memory_57, and memory_91 are now materially less trustworthy than their confident phrasing suggests, because consolidation here demonstrably dropped a retention collapse and an explicit warning. memory_57's 'no measurable harm to retention' and memory_91's engagement-only framing should be read as unaudited. I am not acting on them this week and would verify before doing so.

Two residual uncertainties keep this at standard scale rather than broad rollout. First, exp_86 never reported qualified revenue and exp_31's retention was slightly negative, so the revenue-per-account effect of a shorter flow is inferred, not established. Second, both records predate the competitive shift; a funnel declining under new pressure may not respond as it did on day 12 or 52, and exp_31 explicitly did not replicate outside SMB. So: run on the self-serve SMB segment where both records apply, shorten onboarding steps without deleting qualification fields, and instrument qualified revenue and retention through at least one renewal cycle — the exp_73 lesson is that 30-day numbers can hide a first-renewal cliff. Pre-commit to reading the renewal-window data before any broader rollout, and treat a completion lift with flat or negative qualified revenue as a failure, not a partial win. If the funnel effect proves shallow, activation_messaging is the fallback, but only after memory_91 is verified.
